subject: predictive posterior distribution of a linear regression model using stochastic predictor

messages.author: e1c430550f86b1f6
messages.subject: predictive posterior distribution of a linear regression model using stochastic predictor
parts:
Dear all,

I'm fairly new to STAN and Bayesian stats. So, my apologies if this has been covered elsewhere / wordings are not precise.

Here is the question:

I used STAN to fit a 2-predictors, zero intercept linear model to my data and create a predictive posterior distribution using a new point data.

Stan code as follow:

data {
  int<lower=0> N; // num of obs
  vector[N] y;   
  vector[N] ri;
  vector[N] rc;
  real c_new;
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0> beta_i;
  real<lower=0> beta_c;      
  real<lower=0> sigma;
}
model {
  beta_i ~ normal (1, 2);
  beta_c ~ normal (1, 2.5);

  y ~ normal (ri * beta_i + rc * beta_c, sigma);
}
generated quantities {
  real y_new;
 
  // assume i_new to be 0
  y_new <- normal_rng (c_new * beta_c, sigma);
}

so far so good, using this, i seem to be able to get a posterior distribution based on a supplied value of c_new.

Now, instead of using a single point forecast, c_new. I want to use a normal distribution centered at c_new with externally specified standard deviation.

My question are:
1. Can I just replace y_new with a normal distribution and plug that in? Would there be issues and implicit assumptions (that I should/should not be making)?
2. Is there a better way to do this?

Proposed code:

data {
  int<lower=0> N; // num of obs
  vector[N] y;   
  vector[N] ri;
  vector[N] rc;
  real c_new;  // centre of predictor
  real f_sd;  // sd of predictor
}
generated quantities {
  real s_x;
  real y_new;
 
  s_x <- normal_rng (c_new, f_sd);
  y_new <- normal_rng (s_x * beta_c, sigma);
}

Many thanks in advance!

Andy

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] predictive posterior distribution of a linear regression model using stochastic predictor
parts: See inline.

> On Feb 23, 2015, at 6:26 PM, andy...@cubist-asia.com wrote:
>
> Dear all,
>
> I'm fairly new to STAN and Bayesian stats. So, my apologies if this has been covered elsewhere / wordings are not precise.

I need to add more to the manual on it. I happen to have
one at hand from a tutorial I just taught that lines up
with what you need.

Here's how to do posterior predictive inference in a regression
in Stan:

data {
int<lower=0> N;
vector[N] x;
int<lower=0> y[N];

int<lower=0> M;
vector[M] x_tilde;
}
parameters {
real alpha;
real beta;
real<lower=0> sigma;
}
model {
y ~ poisson(exp(alpha + beta * x));
}
generated quantities {
vector[M] y_tilde;

y_tilde <- normal(alpha + beta * x_tilde, sigma);
}

The idea here is that you have M new items to predict,
with predictors x_tilde ***and noise***.

This is the posterior prediction. You may want to just do this:

y_tilde <- alpha + beta * x_tilde;

which will have the same mean and less noise as it's just predicting
the mean. You will get uncertainty in the alpha and beta estimates.

More below.

> Here is the question:
>
> I used STAN to fit a 2-predictors, zero intercept linear model to my data and create a predictive posterior distribution using a new point data.
>
> Stan code as follow:
>

> real c_new;
> }
> parameters {
> real<lower=0> beta_i;
> real<lower=0> beta_c;
> real<lower=0> sigma;
> }
> model {
> beta_i ~ normal (1, 2);
> beta_c ~ normal (1, 2.5);
>
> y ~ normal (ri * beta_i + rc * beta_c, sigma);
> }
> generated quantities {
> real y_new;
>
> // assume i_new to be 0
> y_new <- normal_rng (c_new * beta_c, sigma);

This doesn't match your model because there's only one
predictor, so I'm a bit confused about what you're trying to do.

> }
>
> so far so good, using this, i seem to be able to get a posterior distribution based on a supplied value of c_new.
>
> Now, instead of using a single point forecast, c_new. I want to use a normal distribution centered at c_new with externally specified standard deviation.

I don't understand why you'd want to do this. You could
make predictions for a bunch of new points, but why a normally
distributed bunch of points?

If you do want to do that, then you need to generate x_tilde randomly.

>
> My question are:
> 1. Can I just replace y_new with a normal distribution and plug that in? Would there be issues and implicit assumptions (that I should/should not be making)?
You could generate random x.
> 2. Is there a better way to do this?

> y_new <- normal_rng (s_x * beta_c, sigma);
> }

Right. That'll work for predicting one new random point.

- Bob

distributed bunch of points?

The idea behind this is as follow:

1. Let's forget ri for a second and assume the model to be fitted y ~ rc + 0
2. I have a  set of y and rc and want to predict y if given rc (predictive distribution with single point rc)
3. But, I actually don't know rc, i only have an estimate rc, e_rc = rc + err.
4. For simplicity, I would model err as N(0, f_sd) - where f_sd would be estimated from another set of data
5. So. the goal is the find the predictive distribution of y given data set (y, rc), new estimate: e_rc and historical error of estimate: f_sd.

Perhaps, there is a much more efficient/elegant way to do this?

If you do want to do that, then you need to generate x_tilde randomly.

My actual application is in financial economics. But, in order to get away with many of the domain specific wordings/issues, let's consider this toy example:

My monthly electricity bill is my outcome: y[1] ... y[N]

Average temperature of the month is my predictor: avg_tmp[1] ... avg_tmp[N]

I use regression to relate the 2 in a linear model (side note: i live in Hong Kong, there is no heating. As temperature heats up, I use more air conditioning, thus driving up the bill. Let's assume usage is linear and unit cost and my behavior being constant (so, no intertemproral dynamics) for this example).

My goal is the predict my electricity bill for month N+1: y_tilde[1]

If i know avg_tmp_tilde[1], it would be straight forward.

But, i don't (and can't) know about it ahead of time.

Instead, let's assume that there is Bob who has made a point(type:real) forecast in each of the past N months in the past:

bob_tmp[1] ... bob_tmp[N]

and for the next month N+1:

bob_tmp_tilde[1]

For simplicity, let's assume Bob's (historical) forecast errors can be described/estimated as:
real bob_sd;
bob_err <- bob_tmp - avg_tmp
bob_err ~ normal (0, bob_sd);

Assume no inter-temporal dynamics, Bob's probabilistic forecast for avg_tmp_tilde[1] should be:

normal(bob_tmp_tilde[1], bob_sd)

Here, I want to know the prediction of y[N+1] given historical relationship, Bob's forecast error history and Bob's forecast for month N+1:

P(y_tilde[1] | avg_tmp[1:N], y[1:N], bob_sd (or bob_tmp[1:N]?), bob_tmp_tilde[1])

To add a bit more complexity to it. 
Let's say Alice, another expert, has also made forecasts (independent of Bob's) in each of the past N months in the past and for the next month N+1:

alice_tmp[1] ... alice_tmp[N]
alice_tmp_tilde[1]

with similar error structure:
real alice_sd;
alice_err <- alice_tmp - avg_tmp
alice_err ~ normal (0, alice_sd);

Similarly, prediction of y[N+1] given historical relationship, Alice's forecast error history and Alice's forecast for month N+1:

P(y_tilde[1] | avg_tmp[1:N], y[1:N], alice_sd (or alice_tmp[1:N]?), alice_tmp_tilde[1])

Assume that I have access only to forecasts made by Bob and Alice. So, my original goal of predicting my electricity bill for month N+1: y_tilde[1] should become:

P(y_tilde[1] | avg_tmp[1:N], y[1:N], bob_sd (or bob_tmp[1:N]?), bob_tmp_tilde[1], alice_sd (or alice_tmp[1:N]?), alice_tmp_tilde[1])

> bob_tmp_tilde[1]
>
> For simplicity, let's assume Bob's (historical) forecast errors can be described/estimated as:
> real bob_sd;
> bob_err <- bob_tmp - avg_tmp
> bob_err ~ normal (0, bob_sd);

I'd write this as

bob_tmp ~ normal(avg_tmp, bob_sd);

But it'll give you the same answer either way. The Gelman and Hill
regression book is great at relating all the notations for all
sorts of models (and even trying to deconstruct what people mean
by "random effect" and "fixed effect").

> Assume no inter-temporal dynamics, Bob's probabilistic forecast for avg_tmp_tilde[1] should be:
>
> normal(bob_tmp_tilde[1], bob_sd)
Right.

> Here, I want to know the prediction of y[N+1] given historical relationship, Bob's forecast error history and Bob's forecast for month N+1:
>
> P(y_tilde[1] | avg_tmp[1:N], y[1:N], bob_sd (or bob_tmp[1:N]?), bob_tmp_tilde[1])

In Stan, the way to write this is this:

y_tilde[1] <- normal_rng(alpha + beta * bob_tmp_tilde[1], y_sd);

This assumes a linear regression with slope and intercept on average
temperate, with y_sd being the error term. Here, bob_tmp_tilde[1] will
be a parameter that's estimated.

If you only care about the posterior mean of y_tilde[1] and not
the uncertainty, then you can drop the normal_rng( , y_sd)
parts.


This is a good example of how Stan behaves as a probabilistic
programming language.

> To add a bit more complexity to it.
> Let's say Alice, another expert, has also made forecasts (independent of Bob's) in each of the past N months in the past and for the next month N+1:
>
> alice_tmp[1] ... alice_tmp[N]
> alice_tmp_tilde[1]
>
> with similar error structure:
> real alice_sd;
> alice_err <- alice_tmp - avg_tmp
> alice_err ~ normal (0, alice_sd);

This won't change anything if you just do the predictions
independently. I'd suggest extending to a hierarchical model
that takes geo-spatial proximity into account. I'm not 100%
sure how to do that without moving to Gaussian processes.

> Similarly, prediction of y[N+1] given historical relationship, Alice's forecast error history and Alice's forecast for month N+1:
>
> P(y_tilde[1] | avg_tmp[1:N], y[1:N], alice_sd (or alice_tmp[1:N]?), alice_tmp_tilde[1])
>
> Assume that I have access only to forecasts made by Bob and Alice. So, my original goal of predicting my electricity bill for month N+1: y_tilde[1] should become:
>
> P(y_tilde[1] | avg_tmp[1:N], y[1:N], bob_sd (or bob_tmp[1:N]?), bob_tmp_tilde[1], alice_sd (or alice_tmp[1:N]?), alice_tmp_tilde[1])
>
> Perhaps, similar problem has been covered in Andrew's book (I'm waiting for it to arrive at my bookstore) or elsewhere?

I'm not sure Gelman and Hill's regression book, or Gelman et al. Bayesian
Data Analysis book covers the case of uncertainty in prediction. It
looks like a measurement error model, but it's not quite a measurement.

- Bob
